--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Simson line

A classical theorem (the **Simson line** theorem) states that if a point \(P\) lies on the circumcircle of a
triangle, then the three feet of the perpendiculars from \(P\) to the sides of the triangle are collinear.
Since \(C\) belongs to the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABD\) (the quadrilateral \(ABCD\) is cyclic), the points
\(E,\;G,\;F\) are collinear:

\[
E,\;G,\;F\ \text{lie on a straight line.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Position of the points on the line

The extra conditions  

\[
BC>DA\qquad\text{and}\qquad AB>CD
\]

guarantee that the perpendiculars from \(C\) meet the **segments** \(AB,\ AD,\ BD\) rather than their
extensions. Consequently the three feet appear on the line in the order  

\[
E\;-\;G\;-\;F .
\]

Thus \(G\) lies between \(E\) and \(F\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The required angle

Because \(E,\;G,\;F\) are collinear and \(G\) is an interior point of the segment \(EF\), the angle formed at
\(G\) by the two rays \(GE\) and \(GF\) is a straight angle:

\[
\angle EGF = 180^{\circ}.
\]
